probes.query: Inside an async transaction block, an ordinary model query is run without naming any connection, yet it executes on the transaction's connection instead of a pooled one. How does that swap happen, where is it recorded per task, and where is it undone?
expectedFacts: TransactionContextPooled.__aenter__ acquires a pool connection and then calls get_connections().set(connection_name, client) to install the transaction client before begin().

ConnectionHandler.set copies the alias-to-client dict, puts the transaction client in the copy and stores it in a ContextVar, so the replacement is visible only to the current asyncio task; it returns a token.

A plain query resolves its connection through QuerySet._choose_db -> model._meta.db -> get_connection(default_connection) -> ConnectionHandler.get, which reads the same ContextVar storage and so returns the transaction client.
TransactionContextPooled.__aexit__ commits or rolls back and, in a finally block, calls get_connections().reset(token) to restore the previous storage.

probes.query: For a model with a datetime column that refreshes itself every time the record is written, at which step of saving an already-stored instance is the current time computed, and what ends up on the object versus what is sent to the database?
expectedFacts: Model.save() on an instance that is already stored (and has a pk) calls executor.execute_update(self, update_fields).
BaseExecutor.execute_update builds the parameter list by calling field.to_db_value(value, instance) for every non-pk, non-generated field.

DatetimeField.to_db_value, when the instance argument is a model instance and auto_now is set (or auto_now_add with a None attribute), computes timezone.localtime(), stores to_python_value(now) on the instance attribute and returns the aware now as the DB value.
The queryset-level update passes None as the instance to to_db_value, so this refresh does not happen there.

probes.query: On MySQL, substring-style text lookups in filters generate different SQL than on other databases. Where is the MySQL-specific replacement declared, and how and when does it get swapped into a model's table of available lookups?
expectedFacts: MySQLExecutor.FILTER_FUNC_OVERRIDE maps the generic contains/starts_with/ends_with and insensitive variants (plus search, json and posix_regex operators) to mysql_* functions that cast the column to CHAR, escape backslash, percent and underscore, and use a StrWrapper.
BaseExecutor.get_overridden_filter_func is a classmethod that looks the generic operator up in the executor class's FILTER_FUNC_OVERRIDE dict.

MetaInfo._generate_filters iterates the model's generic filters and, using the model's default connection's executor_class.get_overridden_filter_func, copies in the overridden operator for each filter that has one.
This runs from MetaInfo.finalise_model, which Apps._build_initial_querysets calls for every model during Tortoise init (only when connections are validated/initialised).

probes.query: When a user runs the command-line command that applies pending schema migrations, how does the tool work out which migration files to run and in what order, and where is the record of already-applied ones kept?
expectedFacts: MigrationLoader.load_disk imports each app's configured migrations package and every non-package module in it whose name does not start with _ or ~, instantiating its Migration class; build_graph adds nodes plus internal and external dependency edges.

MigrationExecutor.migrate loads applied keys from the recorder, then _migration_plan/_forward_plan call graph.forwards_plan(target) (an iterative DFS over parents, so dependencies come first) and skip keys that are already applied.

Applied migrations are stored in a table named tortoise_migrations (app, name, applied_at), read ordered by applied_at via MigrationRecorder.applied_migrations and written with record_applied after each applied step.
The CLI upgrade command calls the same migrate path with direction='forward'.

probes.query: When loading many objects and asking to pre-load a many-to-many relation for all of them, how many extra statements run for that relation, how is the join table used, and how are the loaded rows handed back to each object?
expectedFacts: QuerySet.prefetch_related only records the relation names in _prefetch_map; the work happens after the main SELECT, when execute_select calls _execute_prefetch_queries, which runs one _do_prefetch task per relation concurrently via asyncio.gather.

probes.query: When a single joined SELECT returns a parent record together with the columns of a related record, how are the flat result columns told apart and turned back into a parent object with a nested related object, and what happens when the joined side is empty?
expectedFacts: QuerySet._join_select_related joins the related table and selects the related model's db fields aliased as '<table>.<field>', and appends (related model, column count, field name, parent model, path) tuples to _select_related_idx.
BaseExecutor.execute_select slices each result row positionally using those column counts, strips the table prefix with k.split('.', 1)[1], and builds each related instance with _init_from_db.

probes.query: An application supplies its database password as a function that returns a fresh token instead of a fixed string. For the two PostgreSQL drivers, where is that function actually invoked, and why does the handling differ between them?
expectedFacts: resolve_password in the base client module calls a callable password and awaits the result if it is awaitable, otherwise returns the string/None unchanged.
AsyncpgDBClient.create_connection passes password=self.password straight to asyncpg.create_pool, because asyncpg itself resolves a callable password once per new connection.

PsycopgClient.create_connection passes password=None into make_conninfo when the password is callable and builds a connection subclass (password_factory_connection_class) whose connect() awaits resolve_password(factory) for every new connection, because psycopg bakes credentials into an immutable conninfo string.

probes.query: The convenience that fetches a record matching some criteria or otherwise inserts one can race with another writer. How does it avoid failing or duplicating, and what does it do after losing the race?

probes.query: Where does the migration system refuse to roll back a migration containing steps that have no defined way to be undone, and what decides whether such a step counts as undoable?
expectedFacts: Migration.unapply raises ValueError('Operation ... is not reversible') for any operation whose reversible attribute is false, before any rollback SQL is executed.
Operation.reversible defaults to True; RunPython sets reversible = reverse_code is not None and RunSQL sets reversible = reverse_sql is not None.
If such an operation were run backward anyway, RunPython/RunSQL.database_backward raise NotImplementedError.

probes.query: Where does creating all tables in one shot give up when the tables' foreign keys point at each other in a loop?
expectedFacts: _get_table_sql collects, per table, the set of referenced table names in a 'references' entry.

get_create_schema_sql repeatedly picks a not-yet-created table whose references are a subset of the created tables plus itself (self references are allowed); if none qualifies it raises ConfigurationError('Can't create schema due to cyclic fk references').

probes.query: How are the names of automatically generated database indexes and foreign-key constraints built so that they stay short and stay the same from run to run?
expectedFacts: Index names are '<prefix>_<table[:11]>_<first field[:7]>_<hash>' where the hash is the first 6 hex chars of sha256 over the table name and all field names joined by ';'.
Foreign-key names are 'fk_<from_table[:8]>_<to_table[:8]>_<hash>' with an 8-char sha256 prefix over from_table, from_field, to_table and to_field; truncation is for the 30-character Oracle limit.
The same formula is implemented twice: in the schema generator used by generate_schemas and in the migration schema editor.

probes.query: When a query returns a huge number of rows, how does turning them into model objects avoid starving other coroutines on the event loop, and what controls how often it yields?
expectedFacts: CHUNK_SIZE is a module constant equal to 2000.
In execute_select's row loop, whenever row_idx != 0 and row_idx % CHUNK_SIZE == 0 it awaits asyncio.sleep(0) to yield control to the event loop.
execute_union uses the same pattern.

The offset is computed as datetime.now(tz=get_default_timezone()).utcoffset() and formatted as +H:MM / -H:MM.

probes.query: When updating a column on many already-loaded objects in one call, what shape of SQL does the library generate per batch, and what extra step does it take for PostgreSQL?
expectedFacts: For each batch (chunk of objects) and each field, _make_queries builds a CASE expression with one WHEN pk = <pk> THEN <value> per object, assigns it with SET and adds WHERE pk IN (<batch pks>).
When the schema generator dialect is 'postgres', each THEN value is wrapped in a CAST to the field's dialect SQL_TYPE.
_execute_many runs one statement per batch sequentially and sums the affected-row counts.

probes.query: When a transaction block is opened inside another one on SQLite, how is the inner block realised in SQL, how is it named, and what happens to it on success versus on an exception?
expectedFacts: Inside an active transaction the task's connection is a SqliteTransactionWrapper, whose _in_transaction returns NestedTransactionContext(SqliteTransactionWrapper(self)).
NestedTransactionContext.__aenter__ calls client.savepoint(), which executes SAVEPOINT tortoise_savepoint_<n>, the name coming from a module-level counter in _gen_savepoint_name.
On a clean exit __aexit__ calls release_savepoint (RELEASE <name>); on an exception other than TransactionManagementError it calls savepoint_rollback (ROLLBACK TO <name>).

Contrast asyncpg uses native nested transactions: tortoise/backends/asyncpg/client.py:174-177 (TransactionWrapper._in_transaction -> NestedTransactionContext), :194-195 (savepoint() just calls begin()).

probes.query: Where is the lazily streaming iteration over a very large query result implemented, the kind that keeps a database cursor open and yields rows to the caller in batches?
expectedFacts: No streaming or server-side cursor facility exists; QuerySet.__aiter__ does 'for val in await self', i.e. it materialises the whole result list first.

Drivers fetch complete result sets (fetchall / execute_fetchall); the only large-result mitigation is yielding to the event loop every CHUNK_SIZE (2000) rows in execute_select, and utils.chunk only batches bulk writes.

probes.query: Where can I register a function that runs only after the surrounding transaction has been successfully committed?
